Lightning strikes occur statistically once per year on every commercial aircraft
A typical lightning strike can exceed 200,000 amperes (200 kA) occurring in less than a fraction of a second
Lightning channel temperatures can reach up to 30,000 K locally during a strike
Aircraft grounding for lightning damage repairs can last up to 6 working days
The percentage of composite materials in structural parts of modern passenger aircraft increased from 5% to 50% over the last 50 years
Zone 1A (radome, wingtips, nacelles) experiences the highest lightning currents up to 200 kA
Zone 2 (majority of fuselage) experiences lower currents up to 2 kA
Lightning current discharges of 5-10 kA are the most common according to statistical data
Resistive heating in composite structures can reach several thousand degrees Celsius
Polyaniline (PANI) has semiconductor-level electrical conductivity
Metal mesh and expanded foil (copper and aluminum) are the most frequently selected LSP solutions
Interwoven wire fabrics (IWWF) typically use four mil diameter wires
Plated fiber LSP uses nickel coating which vaporizes during lightning strikes to spread energy density
Carbon nanotube composites have excellent LSP properties but are too expensive for industrial application
The developed organic composite uses epoxy resin as the matrix material
Carbon fiber reinforcement provides additional conducting paths in the organic composite through percolation clusters
UltraConductive coating on carbon composite achieves 121 dB of EMI shielding equivalent to 1-mm thick aluminum skin
SAE ARP 5414A defines 6 lightning strike zones on typical strait-wing jet aircraft
European aviation standards are coordinated through the European Organization for Civil Aviation Electronics (EUROCAE)
Barely visible impact damage (BVID) and visible impact damage (VID) are threshold standards for lightning strike maintenance
Galvanic corrosion can occur between carbon fiber and certain metallic protection materials
Phosphor bronze, aluminum, and copper wires are commonly used in interwoven wire fabric solutions
Debonding at metal-polymer interfaces is a significant failure mode in metallic mesh LSP solutions
The developed organic composite offers comparable electrical properties to metallic mesh solutions with lower density
Manufacturing complexity and cost are critical factors in selecting practical LSP solutions for aircraft
